messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya, a 43-year-old plumber, still remembers the morning that changed everything. She was working on a residential plumbing repair when a corroded pipe burst, releasing a cloud of industrial solvent fumes that had been trapped behind a wall. The smell was acrid, chemical—like scorched plastic and burnt copper. Within seconds her throat burned, her vision blurred, and she collapsed, gasping. Emergency responders pulled her out; she spent three days in the hospital being treated for acute chemical pneumonitis. She was discharged with a clean bill of physical health, but something had lodged itself deep inside her.

Weeks later, Priya could not shake the feeling that the smell was still there. A neighbor's barbecue sent her heart hammering; the faint odor of burnt toast from a coworker's lunch made her break into a cold sweat. What frightened her most was how quickly her body reacted before her mind could catch up—each time, her chest tightened, her palms grew slick, and she felt the urgent need to get away. She had come to believe that any burnt or smoky odor was a sign of immediate danger. Her husband, Ravi, once left an oven mitt on a burner; Priya smelled it from two rooms away and began shaking uncontrollably, certain another toxic cloud was forming.

In response, she began scanning every room she entered—checking corners, sniffing the air, looking for vents or appliances that might leak. She learned to avoid any place where she might be surprised by a smell: busy garages, kitchens near restaurants, even her own home when Ravi cooked. She also started avoiding all feelings, positive or negative, because any strong emotion seemed to lower her defenses and make smells feel more present. She would suppress a laugh, numb a worry, tell herself not to react. When she cut her hand on a pipe fitting and needed stitches, she refused to go to the emergency room, terrified that the antiseptic and bleach smells would send her into a panic. She bandaged it herself, and it festered for days before Ravi insisted she see a doctor. She went only after he promised to keep the car windows open.

Her hypervigilance became a loop that tightened over months. The more alert she remained, the more faint odors she detected—a whiff of diesel from a passing truck, the metallic tang of hot solder in her toolbag—and each new detection became another trigger. She woke several times a night to check the smoke alarm, to sniff the bedroom air, to make sure the heater wasn't glowing. Ravi would find her standing by the window at 2 a.m., breathing deliberately, convinced she smelled something burning. She had started sleeping in the living room because the bedroom vents could carry odors from the kitchen. This constant scanning also made her more sensitive to smells at work; she would stop mid-task to stare at a water heater, sure she detected a chemical leak, even when her apprentice assured her nothing was wrong. Her avoidance of feelings meant she never acknowledged the exhaustion or the fear, and so the cycle continued: the threat she sensed kept the triggers alive, and the triggers demanded yet more scanning and numbing.

By the time she sought help, Priya had lost two jobs—a contractor told her she was too slow because she kept stopping to check the air, and a small residential client complained she refused to work near a gas stove. She was afraid to drive past the hospital where she had been treated, choosing a twenty-minute detour to avoid the smell of its parking deck. She came to therapy because Ravi had given her an ultimatum: he could not watch her shrink away from her own life. What Priya hoped for, more than anything, was to walk into a kitchen without flinching at the scent of a hot pan. But what she feared most was that the smell would never leave her—that she would spend the rest of her days checking, avoiding, and waiting for the next invisible poison to announce itself.
